description: We are a team from Baku, Azerbaijan, taking on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our team combines research and IT: we have a web developer, a designer, and members with experience in space research, science olympiads, and hackathons. We share a passion for astronomy and for making real NASA data accessible to everyone. Our team is complete, and we're excited to build something great together!
summary:
We built Parallax, a free web tool that lets anyone explore real NASA SPHEREx images and look for changes in the sky. Users pick any spot on an interactive sky sphere, and Parallax pulls every SPHEREx frame of it from NASA/IPAC IRSA, labeled by date. With blink, overlay and a difference view, they can catch an object that moved, brightened or appeared. They can check it against the SIMBAD catalog and mark it with a confidence rating.

The challenge asks for a public tool that helps people search SPHEREx data for changes, because no one person can check it all. Parallax answers with citizen science: every find goes to a Community section where others investigate and review it. Results are shown as leads, not proof. A sound mode, where each star has its own tone, adds another way to explore.

Parallax opens the search for Planet X and other moving objects to people outside the field, so a student in Azerbaijan or Brazil can work with the same data as scientists and help decide what deserves a closer look.
details:
The sky never stands still. Now anyone can watch it move.

Somewhere in the outer Solar System, a planet may still be hiding. If it's there, it is faint and slow. It would show up only as a tiny shift between two images taken months apart. NASA's SPHEREx telescope maps the whole sky again and again, so those images already exist. There are just far more of them than any one person can check. Parallax was built for exactly that.

What is Parallax?
Parallax is a free web tool that lets anyone explore real SPHEREx images and look for changes in the sky. It pulls frames from NASA/IPAC IRSA, the archive that holds SPHEREx data, and turns them into something you can browse, compare and discuss. No astronomy degree needed.

How it works

  • Pick a spot. Click anywhere on the interactive sky sphere.
  • Travel in time. Parallax finds every SPHEREx frame of that spot and labels each one with its date.
  • Spot the change. Choose two frames. Fade or blink between them to catch an object that shifted. Or open the difference view: whatever got brighter or fainter between the two dates lights up in red or blue.
  • Identify it. Click a visible object to look it up in the SIMBAD star catalog and see if it's already known.
  • Mark and share. Flag your find as a moving object, a brightness change, something that appeared or disappeared, or a possible artifact. Rate your confidence and send it to the community.

Listen to the sky
Turn the sound on and the sky starts to play. As you move across the map, Parallax plays a tone for the nearest star. Its pitch follows the star's type, so hot and cool stars sound different, and every star keeps its own voice. The tutorial even asks you to recognise a star by ear.

Many eyes on one sky
One person misses things. A crowd misses far less. In the Community section, every find appears as a card with its coordinates and notes. Others open it, investigate it and leave a review. Community agreement isn't scientific confirmation, and Parallax says so openly. What it does is turn an endless archive into a shortlist worth an astronomer's time.

Benefits and impact

  • Citizen science. Anyone, anywhere, can take part in a real search.
  • Easy to start. A short tutorial walks first-time visitors through every tool.
  • Real investigation tools. Blink, overlay, difference view and catalog lookup, all in the browser.

Parallax opens sky exploration, and the search for Planet X, to people outside the field. Students, hobbyists and curious people around the world work on the same data and check each other's finds. Together they can back up promising candidates faster than a small team could alone.

What makes it different
Parallax puts the search and the discussion in one place, right on real SPHEREx images, so a find never stays with one person. And it lets you hear the stars as well as see them.

What we kept in mind

  • An interface a beginner understands at first glance.
  • Objects you can identify one by one, right on the sky map.
  • Honest results: confidence and community agreement are shown as leads, not as proof or a probability of Planet X.
  • Clear credit to NASA SPHEREx and Caltech/IPAC IRSA for every image.

Built with
React, JavaScript, HTML, CSS and Tailwind CSS on the frontend, with Aladin Lite for the interactive sky and the Web Audio API for sound. Node.js, Supabase and SQL run the backend. Vite and Render.com handle building and hosting, and we developed in VS Code with Git. Sky images come from NASA SPHEREx data via NASA/IPAC IRSA, and object lookups use the SIMBAD catalog.

Parallax brings people together from all over the world. People who want to make a difference, but never had a telescope, a lab or a degree to start with. Now they have the same SPHEREx data as the scientists, and each other. The next discovery might come from a classroom in Azerbaijan or a bedroom in Brazil.
